claims.text: Composition-induced variations in stacking-fault energy govern mechanical-property differences among Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its subsets.
Reducing stacking-fault energy favors deformation twinning over dislocation slip.
Deformation twinning increases strain hardening.
Deformation twinning can improve ductility.
All investigated alloys will be fully recrystallized, single-phase FCC materials produced using identical thermomechanical processing.
Selection of quaternary or ternary subsets, or small alloying additions, can be used to tailor stacking-fault energy.
In-situ TEM can document twin formation and dislocation dynamics during mechanical deformation.
The baseline and modified alloys will be tested under identical conditions at approximately 25 °C and 200 °C.
Changes in alloy chemistry alter intrinsic stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy lowers the energetic barrier for twin nucleation.
Higher stacking-fault energy favors dislocation slip and suppresses deformation twinning.
Higher stacking-fault energy produces reduced strain hardening.
A modest stacking-fault-energy reduction will increase deformation-twin density relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
A modest stacking-fault-energy reduction will increase strain-hardening rates relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
A modest stacking-fault-energy reduction will improve ductility relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The predicted ductility improvement will occur without sacrificing strength.
The hypothesis is limited to fully recrystallized, single-phase FCC alloys deformed at moderate strain rates between approximately 25 °C and 200 °C.
Extreme temperatures, non-equilibrium microstructures, and secondary phases may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Stacking-fault energy can be estimated indirectly from diffraction data or peak analysis.
Failure of lower-SFE alloys to show statistically significant increases in twinning, strain hardening, or ductility relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Selection of an equiatomic quaternary or ternary subset is described as a minor compositional modification, although removing one or two 20 at.% constituents and renormalizing the remainder is a major composition change. Only the proposed small alloying additions are clearly minor.
